newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Scores arrested in Cyprus clashes after concert.
newsitem.headline: Scores arrested in Cyprus clashes after concert.

text.p: Calm returned to the Cyprus capital Nicosia on Tuesday after a night of disturbances sparked by Greek Cypriots opposed to a United Nations-sponsored peace concert in the no-man's land dividing the city.

Fifty-five people, including 39 policemen, were slightly injured during nearly three hours of pitched battles between youths and riot police in the heart of the city on Monday night. Fifty-four people were arrested, police said.
"Their aim was to break through the roadblocks and to terrorise people. When that failed they resorted to all this hooliganism," police spokesman Glafcos Xenos told Reuters on Tuesday.

At the site, town workers began cleaning up the streets strewn with smashed window glass, smouldering plastic dumpsters, bricks and stones. Groups of youths, most of them just curious onlookers, remained gathered in the town until the early hours.
"Police are on the alert for any possibility of further incidents," Xenos added.
The bicommunal pop concert took on a political meaning in the face of opposition from various factions on both sides of the divide.

Opposition by Greek Cypriot groups to the free pop concert -- for both Turkish and Greek Cypriots -- was underlined by a protest concert in the Greek Cypriot-populated half of the capital which attracted about 5,000 people -- some 1,000 more than the estimated audience at the peace concert.
The Greek Cypriot groups saw the concert as an attempt to peddle Turkish propaganda while disregarding the fact that Turkish forces still occupy the northern third of the island.
"We believe it is a trap for our people to show that our main problem is not the occupation but AIDS and drugs," said George Hadjicostas, chairman of the Cyprus Motorcyclists Federation (CMF).
Turkey occupied northern Cyprus in 1974 in an invasion sparked by a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
The CMF, which co-organised the protest gathering, condemned the violence which ensued later by isolated groups of youths.

On the Turkish side, witnesses reported far-right Turkish "Grey Wolf" nationalists threw stones at a bus carrying a Turkish singer to join a Greek pop star at the peace concert. Windows were broken but there were no injuries, they said.

Back in the south, demonstrators smashed windows of police cars and threw at least two petrol bombs. Trash bins were set on fire and protesters lobbed stones at police which responded with tear gas and mass arrests.

In stark contrast to these violent scenes, pop stars Burak Kut of Turkey and Sakis Rouvas of Greece sang for the crowd of young people in the U.N.-controlled no-man's land beside the Venetian walls that had once protected the city.

Singing a mixture of Greek and Turkish songs, and several in English, the two singers drew cheers from the crowd as they hugged one another and shook hands at the end of the concert, which lasted about 90 minutes.
"This conveyed a positive message to politicians to find a peaceful solution to this problem," said Rouvas at a news conference with Kut held immediately after the concert.
"I am sorry about some people who believe in what they are doing and resort to some means which cause disturbance," he said, referring to the incidents.
"In the long run this (concert) will have beneficial effects," Kut added.

The only hiccup to the concert, held in an abandoned football pitch, was when a Turkish member of the crowd lifted his arm and displayed the sign of the Grey Wolves group. The spectator was escorted away from the site by U.N. soldiers.
